claim: In the vertebrate CNS, afferent sensory inputs are targeted to specific depths or layers of their target neuropil.
source: In the vertebrate CNS, afferent sensory inputs are targeted to specific depths or layers of their target neuropil.
evidence: This is a general statement about vertebrate CNS organization that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Laminar patterning of sensory inputs exists ab initio, from the very beginning, and has been considered an activity-independent process.
source: This patterning exists ab initio, from the very beginning, and therefore has been considered an activity-independent process.
evidence: This claim references the prevailing view in the field about activity-independence of laminar patterning.

claim: The subcellular segregation of visual and mechanosensory inputs to specific regions of tectal neuron dendrites in the tadpole optic tectum requires NMDA receptor activity.
source: However, here we report that, during circuit development, the subcellular segregation of the visual and mechanosensory inputs to specific regions of tectal neuron dendrites in the tadpole optic tectum requires NMDA receptor activity.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from NMDAR blockade experiments showing disrupted segregation.

claim: Blocking NMDARs during the formation of sensory circuits leads to less defined segregation.
source: Blocking NMDARs during the formation of these sensory circuits, or removing the visual set of inputs, leads to less defined segregation, and suggests a correlation-based mechanism in which correlated inputs wire to common regions of dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing altered segregation patterns when MK-801 is applied during circuit formation.

claim: Removing the visual set of inputs leads to less defined segregation.
source: Blocking NMDARs during the formation of these sensory circuits, or removing the visual set of inputs, leads to less defined segregation, and suggests a correlation-based mechanism in which correlated inputs wire to common regions of dendrites.
evidence: This claim is supported by monocular enucleation experiments showing HB inputs extending into RGC territory.

claim: A correlation-based mechanism exists in which correlated inputs wire to common regions of dendrites.
source: Blocking NMDARs during the formation of these sensory circuits, or removing the visual set of inputs, leads to less defined segregation, and suggests a correlation-based mechanism in which correlated inputs wire to common regions of dendrites.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the experimental results and known NMDAR function.

claim: Blocking NMDA receptors during later stages of circuit development did not disrupt segregation.
source: Blocking NMDA receptors during later stages of circuit development did not disrupt segregation, indicating a critical period for activity-dependent shaping of patterns of innervation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that MK-801 exposure at stage 45 does not affect segregation.

claim: There is a critical period for activity-dependent shaping of patterns of innervation.
source: Blocking NMDA receptors during later stages of circuit development did not disrupt segregation, indicating a critical period for activity-dependent shaping of patterns of innervation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of early versus late NMDAR blockade.

claim: Different sensory inputs to the optic tecta of birds form distinct layers across the laminar axis.
source: For example, the different sensory inputs that are received and processed by the optic tecta of birds (Acheson et al., 1980; Yamagata et al., 1995), fish (Xiao et al., 2005; Xiao and Baier, 2007), and amphibians (Harris, 1982, 1983; Udin and Fawcett, 1988; Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009), and the superior colliculus of mammals (May, 2006; Wallace et al., 1993; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Inayat et al., 2015), form distinct layers across the laminar axis of their target neuropil.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different sensory inputs to the optic tecta of fish form distinct layers across the laminar axis.
source: For example, the different sensory inputs that are received and processed by the optic tecta of birds (Acheson et al., 1980; Yamagata et al., 1995), fish (Xiao et al., 2005; Xiao and Baier, 2007), and amphibians (Harris, 1982, 1983; Udin and Fawcett, 1988; Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009), and the superior colliculus of mammals (May, 2006; Wallace et al., 1993; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Inayat et al., 2015), form distinct layers across the laminar axis of their target neuropil.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different sensory inputs to the optic tecta of amphibians form distinct layers across the laminar axis.
source: For example, the different sensory inputs that are received and processed by the optic tecta of birds (Acheson et al., 1980; Yamagata et al., 1995), fish (Xiao et al., 2005; Xiao and Baier, 2007), and amphibians (Harris, 1982, 1983; Udin and Fawcett, 1988; Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009), and the superior colliculus of mammals (May, 2006; Wallace et al., 1993; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Inayat et al., 2015), form distinct layers across the laminar axis of their target neuropil.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Different sensory inputs to the superior colliculus of mammals form distinct layers across the laminar axis.
source: For example, the different sensory inputs that are received and processed by the optic tecta of birds (Acheson et al., 1980; Yamagata et al., 1995), fish (Xiao et al., 2005; Xiao and Baier, 2007), and amphibians (Harris, 1982, 1983; Udin and Fawcett, 1988; Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009), and the superior colliculus of mammals (May, 2006; Wallace et al., 1993; Cang and Feldheim, 2013; Inayat et al., 2015), form distinct layers across the laminar axis of their target neuropil.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), retinal ganglion cell input is segregated into eye-specific layers.
source: In the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), retinal ganglion cell input is segregated into eye-specific layers (Rakic, 1976; Linden et al., 1981; Shatz, 1983)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the hippocampus, entorhinal cortical input forms synaptic connections onto the distal regions of hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: and in the hippocampus, entorhinal cortical input forms synaptic connections onto specifically the distal regions of hippocampal pyramidal neurons, while the commissural inputs from within the hippocampus synapse onto the proximal portions of the same dendrites (Supèr and Soriano, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the hippocampus, commissural inputs from within the hippocampus synapse onto the proximal portions of pyramidal neuron dendrites.
source: and in the hippocampus, entorhinal cortical input forms synaptic connections onto specifically the distal regions of hippocampal pyramidal neurons, while the commissural inputs from within the hippocampus synapse onto the proximal portions of the same dendrites (Supèr and Soriano, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Eye-dependent segregation of inputs to the LGN are initially overlapping and then become segregated into layers by activity-dependent mechanisms.
source: With the exception of the eye-dependent segregation of inputs to the LGN, which are initially overlapping with one another and then become segregated or refined into layers by activity-dependent mechanisms, most lamination of inputs appears to exist ab initio, from the beginning, before sensory-driven activity is present, and therefore is considered to be an activity-independent process (Huberman et al., 2010; Xiao and Baier, 2007; Xiao et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Most lamination of inputs appears to exist ab initio, before sensory-driven activity is present.
source: With the exception of the eye-dependent segregation of inputs to the LGN, which are initially overlapping with one another and then become segregated or refined into layers by activity-dependent mechanisms, most lamination of inputs appears to exist ab initio, from the beginning, before sensory-driven activity is present, and therefore is considered to be an activity-independent process (Huberman et al., 2010; Xiao and Baier, 2007; Xiao et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Xenopus tadpole optic tectum is a multisensory integration center.
source: For this we use the Xenopus tadpole optic tectum as a model system, a relatively simple and well-studied multisensory integration center.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tadpole optic tectum.

claim: The optic tectum receives direct visual input from the retinal ganglion cells in the eye.
source: The optic tectum receives direct visual input from the retinal ganglion cells in the eye and mechanosensory input that enters the tectum via the brainstem.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tadpole optic tectum.

claim: The optic tectum receives mechanosensory input that enters the tectum via the brainstem.
source: The optic tectum receives direct visual input from the retinal ganglion cells in the eye and mechanosensory input that enters the tectum via the brainstem.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tadpole optic tectum.

claim: Visual and mechanosensory inputs form topographic maps parallel with the surface of the neuropil.
source: Both sets of afferent sensory inputs form topographic maps parallel with the surface of the neuropil, (Sperry, 1963; Holt and Harris, 1983; Sakaguchi and Murphey, 1985; Udin and Fawcett, 1988; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Visual inputs innervate the distal-most neuropil of the optic tectum.
source: These maps are segregated from one another such that visual inputs innervate the distal-most neuropil and mechanosensory inputs innervate the proximal-most layer, the region closest to the somata of the tectal neurons (Hiramoto and Cline, 2009; Hamodi and Pratt, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mechanosensory inputs innervate the proximal-most layer of the optic tectum, the region closest to the somata of the tectal neurons.
source: These maps are segregated from one another such that visual inputs innervate the distal-most neuropil and mechanosensory inputs innervate the proximal-most layer, the region closest to the somata of the tectal neurons (Hiramoto and Cline, 2009; Hamodi and Pratt, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both visual and mechanosensory inputs are glutamatergic.
source: Both sets of sensory inputs are glutamatergic and activate postsynaptic responses via AMPA and NMDA receptors expressed on tectal neuron dendrites (Wu et al., 1996; Deeg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Visual and mechanosensory inputs activate postsynaptic responses via AMPA and NMDA receptors expressed on tectal neuron dendrites.
source: Both sets of sensory inputs are glutamatergic and activate postsynaptic responses via AMPA and NMDA receptors expressed on tectal neuron dendrites (Wu et al., 1996; Deeg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Deep-layer tectal neuron dendrites extend the entire length of the laminar axis.
source: At the stages studied here, deep-layer tectal neuron dendrites extend the entire length of the laminar axis (Lázár, 1973; Wu and Cline, 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Single tectal neurons are directly innervated by both visual and non-visual inputs.
source: and it is well established that single tectal neurons are directly innervated by both visual and non-visual inputs (Pratt and Aizenman, 2009; Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RGC axons are labeled with DiD (green) and appear confined to distal lamina.
source: First, we confirmed this finding by labeling the RGC axons of stage 48/49 tadpoles with DiD (green), HB inputs with DiI (red), and imaging their terminations in the tectum (Figure 1B–D). We observed that, as previously reported, the two different sensory inputs innervate distinct, non-overlapping lamina in the neuropil with RGC inputs confined to distal lamina, HB inputs to the proximal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from axon labeling and imaging shown in Figure 1.

claim: HB inputs are labeled with DiI (red) and appear confined to proximal lamina.
source: First, we confirmed this finding by labeling the RGC axons of stage 48/49 tadpoles with DiD (green), HB inputs with DiI (red), and imaging their terminations in the tectum (Figure 1B–D). We observed that, as previously reported, the two different sensory inputs innervate distinct, non-overlapping lamina in the neuropil with RGC inputs confined to distal lamina, HB inputs to the proximal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from axon labeling and imaging shown in Figure 1.

claim: The two different sensory inputs innervate distinct, non-overlapping lamina in the neuropil.
source: We observed that, as previously reported, the two different sensory inputs innervate distinct, non-overlapping lamina in the neuropil with RGC inputs confined to distal lamina, HB inputs to the proximal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from axon labeling and imaging shown in Figure 1.

claim: Deep-layer tectal neurons display monosynaptic responses to both RGC and HB input activation.
source: On the postsynaptic side, deep-layer tectal neurons display monosynaptic responses to both RGC and HB input activation (Hamodi and Pratt, 2015; Deeg et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both RGC- and HB-evoked responses include a temporally distinct monosynaptic response followed by a polysynaptic portion.
source: Both evoked responses include a temporally distinct monosynaptic response due to the direct synaptic activation by the afferent input, followed by the polysynaptic portion of the response due to the activation of local microcircuitry within the tectum.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of tectal neuron responses and is illustrated in Figure 1E.

claim: The pattern and strength of RGC and HB-evoked responses recorded from tectal neurons of the modified preparation do not differ from that recorded in the traditional preparation.
source: It was previously established that the pattern and strength of RGC and HB-evoked responses recorded from tectal neurons of the modified preparation do not differ from that recorded in the traditional preparation, indicating that RGC and HB inputs are not severed in the modified brain preparation (Hamodi and Pratt, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The major sink appearing at the far distal end of the neuropil is a characteristic of the RGC-evoked image plot observed for normal tecta.
source: The major sink appearing at the far distal end of the neuropil is a characteristic of the RGC-evoked image plot observed for normal tecta.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The HB-evoked response is characterized by the maximum FP and CSD sink occurring at the proximal end of the laminar axis.
source: The HB-evoked response is characterized by the maximum FP and CSD sink occurring at the proximal end of the laminar axis (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for an example of an HB-evoked FPs, CSDs, and resulting image plot).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The microcircuitry displays a spatially organized, stratified pattern that closely matches that of the monosynaptic pattern.
source: It is interesting to note that the microcircuitry also displays a spatially organized, stratified pattern that closely matches that of the monosynaptic pattern.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the CSD image plots shown in Figure 2D.

claim: RGC and HB afferent inputs begin innervating the tectum simultaneously.
source: It has previously been shown that the RGC and HB afferent inputs begin innervating the tectum simultaneously (Hiramoto and Cline, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Monocular enucleation was performed at stage 34, when RGC axons have just begun to exit the eyecup.
source: To test this, we eliminated the RGC input to one of the two tectal lobes by surgically removing the contralateral eye at stage 34, the stage when RGC axons have just begun to exit the eyecup (Hocking and Mcfarlane, 2007; de La Torre et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies about RGC development.

claim: During early larval stages, the major source of visual input received by the tectum is from the contralateral eye.
source: During the early larval stages of tadpole development which we focus on in this study, the major source of visual input received by the tectum is from the contralateral eye.
evidence: This is established knowledge about tadpole visual system development.

claim: Removing the contralateral eye is an effective method to eliminate the majority of RGC input received by that tectum.
source: Thus removing the contralateral eye is an effective method to eliminate the majority of RGC input received by that tectum.
evidence: This is inferred from the knowledge that the contralateral eye provides the major visual input.

claim: Sparse ipsilateral RGC input has been observed in tadpoles at early larval stages.
source: Occasionally, sparse ipsilateral RGC input has been observed in tadpoles at these stages (Munz et al., 2014); and we, too, have observed the presence of sparse ipsilateral input innervating control tecta and tecta whose contralateral input has been removed via enucleation (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study and the authors' own observations.

claim: The averaged spatial pattern of HB-evoked FPs in the tecta devoid of contralateral RGC input was shifted distally compared to control.
source: Compared to control, we found that the averaged spatial pattern of HB-evoked FPs in the tecta devoid of contralateral RGC input was shifted distally (Figure 3B; distance from distal edge of average HB-evoked FP maximum peak amplitude for control tecta: 110 μm, n = 10, for DCR tecta: 80 μm, n = 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The maximum HB-evoked FP amplitude occurred at a significantly more distal location in the DCR tecta relative to control tecta.
source: In addition, we also identified, for each tectum, the position across the axis where the absolute maximum HB-evoked FP amplitude occurred and found that it occurred at a significantly more distal location in the DCR tecta relative to control tecta (Figure 3C; average distance from distal edge where HB-evoked FP amplitude peaks for control tectum: 104 ± 6.7 μm, n = 10 tecta, 95% Confidence Interval (CI): upper limit = 117.13 μm, lower limit = 90.87 μm; DCR tectum: 84.17 ± 5.29 μm, n = 12 tecta; 95% CI: upper limit = 94.53 μm, lower limit = 73.6 μm p=0.028, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In DCR tecta, the major HB-evoked current sinks appear at more distal locations along the laminar axis compared to control.
source: In the DCR tecta, however, the major HB-evoked current sinks appear at more distal locations along the laminar axis, and in some cases appeared to be widely spread out across the entire length of the laminar axis (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The absence of RGC input causes HB inputs to innervate more distal regions of the laminar axis compared to control.
source: Averaging the distances from the distal edge at which the major HB-evoked CSD sink occurred for both control and DCR tecta indicated, similar to the FP data, that absence of RGC input causes HB inputs to innervate more distal regions of the laminar axis compared to control (Figure 3F; for control tectum, the major HB-evoked CSD sink occurred, on average, at 85 ± 6.9 μm from the distal edge, n = 10 tecta, 95% Confidence Interval (CI) upper limit = 98.5 μm, lower limit = 71.48 μm; for DCR tectum: 69.2 ± 3.6 μm, n = 12 tecta; 95% CI: upper limit = 76.26 μm, lower limit = 62.14 μm p=0.04, unpaired t-test.)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: HB axonal inputs in the DCR tecta appeared less focused in space and extended into the vacant dendritic region that is normally occupied by RGC axons.
source: As predicted by the CSD and FP data, we observed that HB axonal inputs in the DCR tecta appeared less focused in space and extended into the vacant dendritic region that is normally occupied by RGC axons, whereas the control tectum showed a typical confined band of HB axons along the proximal part of the laminar axis (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from axon imaging shown in Figure 4.

claim: Peak fluorescence of control HB axons occurred at 88.6 ± 2.9 μm from the distal edge of the tectum.
source: Peak fluorescence of control HB axons was found to occur, on average, at 88.6 ± 2.9 μm from the distal edge of the tectum (Figure 4E; n = 4 tecta, 95% CI upper limit = 97.9 μm, Cl lower limit = 79.2 μm)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Peak fluorescence of HB axons innervating a DCR tectum occurred at 65.8 ± 4.3 μm from the distal edge.
source: while the peak fluorescence observed for HB axons innervating a DCR tectum occurred at 65.8 ± 4.3 μm from the distal edge (n = 4 tecta, 95% Cl upper limit = 79.4 μm, Cl lower limit = 52.1 μm).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The difference in locations of peak HB axon fluorescence between control and DCR tecta was statistically significant (p=0.004).
source: The difference in locations of peak HB axon fluorescence between control and DCR tecta was statistically significant (p=0.004, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The absence of RGC input does not result in HB inputs taking over the entire distal lamina.
source: We also observed that the absence of RGC input does not result in HB inputs taking over the entire distal lamina, but rather it induces them to take over a fraction of the synaptic sites beyond their distal border, sites that would normally be occupied by retinotectal synapses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from the enucleation experiments.

claim: There is a competition-based interaction at the border/interface between the distal and the proximal portion of the laminar axis.
source: This suggests a competition-based interaction at the border/interface between the distal and the proximal portion of the laminar axis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HB inputs partially invade RGC territory when RGC inputs are absent.

claim: Blocking NMDARs during the formation of the retinotectal projection prevents refinement of the topographic map.
source: It has been established that blocking NMDARs during the formation of the retinotectal projection prevents refinement of the topographic map (Dong et al., 2009; Cline and Constantine-Paton, 1989)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blocking NMDARs prevents the formation of eye-specific stripes in the 3-eyed frog.
source: and the formation of eye-specific stripes in the 3-eyed frog (Cline et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Tadpoles were reared in the presence of the non-competitive NMDAR blocker, MK-801 (25 μM).
source: To determine whether NMDAR blockade disrupts the subcellular targeting of RGC and HB input to the distal and proximal regions, respectively, of tectal neuron dendrites, tadpoles were reared in the presence of the non-competitive NMDAR blocker, MK-801 (25 μM).
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation used in the study.

claim: MK-801 at 25 μM abolishes NMDAR-mediated visual responses in tectal neurons.
source: Adding this drug to the rearing solution chronically inhibits NMDAR activity in tadpoles and it is well established that this drug at this concentration abolishes NMDAR-mediated visual responses in tectal neurons (Ruthazer et al., 2003; Dong et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MK-801 does not significantly alter RGC- or HB-evoked transmission.
source: but does not appear to significantly alter RGC- or HB-evoked transmission (data not shown), consistent with the observation that both RGC and HB-evoked input received by tectal neurons is mediated largely via AMPA receptors (Deeg et al., 2009) and that the presence of MK801 had negligible effects on RGC-evoked responses in tectal neurons (Ruthazer et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' data and citations to previous studies.

claim: RGC and HB-evoked input received by tectal neurons is mediated largely via AMPA receptors.
source: consistent with the observation that both RGC and HB-evoked input received by tectal neurons is mediated largely via AMPA receptors (Deeg et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Exposure to MK-801 began at developmental stage 39, when RGC axons have just reached the tectum.
source: Exposure to the blocker began at developmental stage 39, when RGC axons have just reached the tectum, through stage 49, when the retinotectal circuitry has formed and has undergone some degree of topographic refinement.
evidence: This describes the timing of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The MK-801 treated tecta displayed a noticeably different spatial pattern of both RGC- and HB-evoked FP amplitudes compared to controls.
source: We found that the MK-801 treated tecta displayed a noticeably different spatial pattern of both RGC- and HB-evoked FP amplitudes (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: For controls, the maximum RGC-evoked FP amplitudes occurred at 56.66 ± 7.41 μm from the distal edge.
source: We found that for controls, the maximum RGC-evoked FP amplitudes occurred at 56.66 ± 7.41 μm from the distal edge, n = 15, 95% CI: upper limit = 72.6 μm, lower limit = 40.8 μm
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: For controls, maximum HB-evoked amplitudes occurred at 102.73 ± 5.41 μm from the distal edge.
source: and maximum HB-evoked amplitudes occurred at 102.73 ± 5.41 μm from the distal edge, n = 11, 95% CI: upper limit = 114.8 μm, lower limit = 90.7 μm; p=0.0007, non-parametric Mann-Whitney test (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For controls, approximately 45 μm separates the maximum responses of the two inputs.
source: thus a distance of approximately 45 μm separates the maximum responses of the two inputs.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data.

claim: For MK-801-reared tecta, the maximum RGC-evoked FP amplitudes occurred at 80.48 ± 6.88 μm from the distal edge.
source: For MK-801-reared tecta, the maximum RGC-evoked FP amplitudes occurred at 80.48 ± 6.88 μm from the distal edge, n = 21, 95% CI: upper limit = 94.8 μm, lower limit = 66.1 μm
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: For MK-801-reared tecta, maximum HB-evoked amplitudes occurred at 97.5 ± 7.4 μm from the distal edge.
source: and maximum HB-evoked amplitudes occurred at 97.5 ± 7.4 μm from the distal edge, n = 12, 95% CI: upper limit = 113.8 μm, lower limit = 81.2 μm; p=0.122, unpaired t-test (Figure 5C)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: For MK-801-reared tecta, approximately 17 μm separates the maximum responses of the two inputs.
source: thus a distance of approximately 17 μm separating them.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data.

claim: There is significantly more overlap between RGC and HB in the MK-801 exposed tecta compared to the control tecta.
source: Because of this, we also measured the amount of overlap between the HB- and RGC- evoked FP spatial profiles and observed significantly more overlap between RGC and HB in the MK-801 exposed tecta compared to the control tecta (Figure 5D; overlap index for control: 3.23 ± 0.42, n = 12, 95% CI: upper limit = 4.2 μm, lower limit = 2.3 μm; MK801: 4.42 ± 0.29, n = 12, 95% CI: upper limit = 5.1 μm, lower limit = 3.8 μm; p=0.029, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In control tecta, the main RGC-evoked current sink is localized to the distal region of the laminar axis.
source: In control tecta, the main RGC-evoked current sink is localized to the distal region of the laminar axis (Figure 6A), the HB-evoked current sink to the proximal region (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In control tecta, the HB-evoked current sink is localized to the proximal region.
source: In control tecta, the main RGC-evoked current sink is localized to the distal region of the laminar axis (Figure 6A), the HB-evoked current sink to the proximal region (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In MK-801 reared tadpoles, the RGC- and HB-evoked current sinks appear more diffuse in space.
source: In MK-801 reared tadpoles, however, the RGC- and HB-evoked current sinks appear more diffuse is space and in some cases sinks and sources appeared throughout the entire length of the laminar axis (Figure 6C,D), indicating a disorganized projection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: For control tecta, the maximum RGC-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 50.5 ± 8.9 μm from the distal edge.
source: For control, the maximum RGC-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 50.5 ± 8.9 μm from distal the distal edge (n = 18 tecta; 95% Cl upper limit = 97.94 μm, Cl lower limit = 63.6 μm)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: For control tecta, major HB-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 80.8 ± 7.9 μm from the distal edge.
source: and major HB-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 80.8 ± 7.9 μm from the distal edge (n = 13 tecta; 95% Cl upper limit = 69.28 μm, Cl lower limit = 31.83 μm).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: For control tecta, the average distance between the major HB- and RGC-evoked CSD sinks was statistically significant (p=0.02).
source: The average distance between the major HB- and RGC-evoked CSD sinks was statistically significant (p=0.02, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: For MK-801 tecta, the maximum RGC-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 71.7 ± 9.6 μm from the distal edge.
source: For MK-801 tecta, the maximum RGC-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 71.7 ± 9.6 μm from the distal edge (n = 18 tecta, 95% CI upper limit = 92.01 μm, lower limit = 51.32 μm)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: For MK-801 tecta, the major HB-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 70 ± 8.4 μm from the distal edge.
source: and the major HB-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 70 ± 8.4 μm from the distal edge (n = 11 tecta; 95% Cl upper limit = 88.76 μm, lower limit = 51.24 μm) suggesting essentially no gap, between the inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: For MK-801 tecta, the average distance between the major RGC and HB CSD sinks was not statistically significant (p=0.91).
source: Indeed, the average distance between the major RGC and HB CSD sinks in the MK-801 treated group was not statistically significant (p=0.91, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The majority of the RGC synaptic input in MK801-treated tecta was happening further away from the distal edge compared to control.
source: Thus, the majority of the RGC synaptic input in MK801-treated tecta was happening further away from the distal edge compared to control, and the majority of the HB synaptic input was happening closer to the distal edge compared to control.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The majority of the HB synaptic input in MK801-treated tecta was happening closer to the distal edge compared to control.
source: Thus, the majority of the RGC synaptic input in MK801-treated tecta was happening further away from the distal edge compared to control, and the majority of the HB synaptic input was happening closer to the distal edge compared to control.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Tadpoles were exposed to MK-801 at stage 45, after both the visual and non-visual inputs have established their postsynaptic targets.
source: To address this, tadpoles were exposed to MK-801 at a later stage in development (stage 45), after both the visual and non-visual inputs have established their postsynaptic targets.
evidence: This describes the timing of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The RGC- and HB-evoked spatial profile of peak FP amplitudes of the MK-801-exposed tecta (stage 45 exposure) resemble control profiles.
source: The RGC- and HB-evoked spatial profile of peak FP amplitudes of the MK-801-exposed tecta resemble control profiles (Figure 7A)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The maximum FP amplitude for both RGC and HB inputs occurred at approximately 40 and 100 μm, respectively, from the distal edge for both MK-801 (stage 45 exposure) and control tecta.
source: and we found that the maximum FP amplitude for both RGC and HB inputs occurred at approximately 40 and 100 μm, respectively, from the distal edge of the neuropil for both MK-801 and batch-matched control tecta (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The distance between the maximum RGC-evoked and HB-evoked FP amplitudes is significant for MK-801 tecta exposed at stage 45.
source: Furthermore, the distance between the maximum RGC-evoked and HB-evoked FP amplitudes is significant for both MK-801 (Figure 7B; RGC distance = 46±2.44 μm, 95% CI: upper limit = 52.8 μm, lower limit = 39.2 μm; HB distance = 100±3.16 μm, n = 5; 95% CI: upper limit = 108.8 μm, lower limit = 91.2 μm; p=0.01, non-parametric Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The distance between the maximum RGC-evoked and HB-evoked FP amplitudes is significant for control tecta.
source: and control tecta (Figure 7B; RGC distance = 53.33±13.33 μm, 95% CI: upper limit = 110.7 μm, lower limit = −4 μm; HB distance = 110±7.07 μm; n = 3, 95% CI: upper limit = 132.5 μm, lower limit = 87.5 μm; p=0.047, non-parametric Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: NMDAR activation at stage 45 is not required for the proper segregation of multisensory axons along the laminar axis of the neuropil.
source: indicating that NMDAR activation at stage 45 is not required for the proper segregation of multisensory axons along the laminar axis of the neuropil.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of late MK-801 exposure on segregation.

claim: The main RGC-evoked sinks were localized to the distal portion of the neuropil in tadpoles exposed to MK-801 at stage 45.
source: Analysis of CSDs reveals that, similar to control tecta, the main RGC-evoked sinks were localized to the distal portion of the neuropil (Figure 7C), the HB sinks to the proximal portion, in tadpoles exposed to MK-801 later in development (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The HB sinks were localized to the proximal portion in tadpoles exposed to MK-801 at stage 45.
source: Analysis of CSDs reveals that, similar to control tecta, the main RGC-evoked sinks were localized to the distal portion of the neuropil (Figure 7C), the HB sinks to the proximal portion, in tadpoles exposed to MK-801 later in development (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The distance between the major RGC- and HB-evoked sink was significant for control tecta.
source: Statistical analysis of CSDs indicated that the distance between the major RGC- and HB-evoked sink was significant for both control tecta and the tecta of tadpoles that had been exposed to MK-801 between stages 45 and 49 (Figure 7E). For control tecta, the major RGC-evoked CSD sink occurred at an average of 26.6 ± 16.6 μm from distal the distal edge (n = 3 tecta; 95% Cl upper limit = 98.38 μm, Cl lower limit = 45.04 μm), and the major HB-evoked CSD sink occurred at an average of 92.5 ± 11.1 μm from the distal edge (n = 4 tecta; 95% Cl upper limit = 127.8 μm, Cl lower limit = 57.22 μm). The average distance between the major HB- and RGC-evoked CSD sinks was statistically significant (p=0.018, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The distance between the major RGC- and HB-evoked sink was significant for tecta exposed to MK-801 between stages 45 and 49.
source: For tadpoles exposed to MK-801 between stage 45 and 49, the maximum RGC-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 40 ± 5.5 μm from distal the distal edge (n = 5 tecta, 95% CI upper limit = 55.21 μm, lower limit = 24.79 μm), and the major HB-evoked CSD sinks occurred at an average of 74 ± 5.1 μm from the distal edge (n = 5 tecta; 95% Cl upper limit = 88.2 μm, lower limit = 59.84 μm). This distance between the major RGC- and HB-evoked CSDs was statistically significant (p=0.002, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Blocking NMDARs early during circuit development (stage 39) shortened the average distance between peak RGC and HB axon fluorescence.
source: Compared to control, blocking NMDARs early during circuit development (stage 39) shortened the average distance between peak RGC and HB axon fluorescence (Figure 8A,B and D; distance between peak fluorescence for RGC and HB axons for control tecta: 57.1 ± 4.0 μm, n = 5, 95% Cl upper limit = 65.58 μm, Cl lower limit = 52.62 μm; for early MK-801 tecta: 40.45 ± 2.15 μm, n = 11 tecta; 95% Cl upper limit = 47.23 μm, Cl lower limit = 34.54 μm; p=0.001 compared to control distance; unpaired t-test)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Blocking NMDARs later in development (stage 45) did not significantly affect the distance between peak RGC and HB axon fluorescence.
source: while blocking NMDARs later in development (stage 45) did not appear to elicit a significant effect on this distance (Figure 8C and D; late MK-801 tecta: 50.8 ± 7.0 μm, n = 5, 95% Cl upper limit = 70.18 μm, Cl lower limit = 31.42 μm; p=0.45 compared to control distance, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Early and late NMDAR blockade significantly increased the total amount of overlap of RGC and HB axons compared to control.
source: We found that early and late NMDAR blockade significantly increased the total amount of overlap of RGC and HB axons compared to control (Figure 8A–C and E; the average RGC and HB overlap area for control: 12.5 ± 1.7 gray value * μm, n = 7, 95% Cl upper limit = 15.82, Cl lower limit = 9.19 gray value * μm; for early MK-801 tecta: 23.1 ± 3.7 gray value * μm, n = 11, 95% Cl upper limit = 30.3, Cl lower limit = 15.9 gray value * μm; p=0.04 compared to control, un-paired t-test; for late MK-801 tecta: 29.85 ± 4.4 gray value * μm, n = 5, 95% Cl upper limit = 38.4, Cl lower limit = 21.3 gray value * μm; p=0.002 compared to control).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Blocking NMDARs later in development did not disrupt the distance between peak FPS, CSDs, or axon fluorescence, but did increase overlap.
source: Thus, although blocking NMDARs later in development did not disrupt the distance between peak FPS, CSDs, or axon fluorescence, it did appear to activate a fraction of axons – perhaps a set of relatively immature axons that are still undergoing NMDAR-dependent processes – to desegregate.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data comparing early and late MK-801 effects.

claim: Once formed and likely stabilized via NMDAR-dependent mechanisms, sensory-specific axon segregation is no longer NMDAR-dependent for the majority of axons.
source: Combined, these data suggest that, once formed and likely stabilized via NMDAR-dependent mechanisms, sensory-specific axon segregation is no longer NMDAR-dependent for the majority of axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of early versus late NMDAR blockade.

claim: There is a critical period or window in developmental time in which the inputs will shift across the laminar axis in the absence of NMDAR activity.
source: Thus, there appears to be a critical period or window in developmental time in which the inputs will shift across the laminar axis in the absence of NMDAR activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of early versus late NMDAR blockade.

claim: During the development of the Xenopus tadpole tectal circuitry, absence of RGC axons in the optic tectum causes the mechanosensory inputs to shift distally along the laminar axis of the neuropil.
source: The major findings of this study are (1) During the development of the Xenopus tadpole tectal circuitry, absence of RGC axons in the optic tectum causes the mechanosensory inputs to shift distally along the laminar axis of the neuropil such that a fraction of these inputs move into the neighboring vacant lamina and form synaptic connections with distal dendrites that are normally dendritic region innervated by RGC inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the enucleation experiments.

claim: Chronic blockade of NMDA receptors during circuit development desegregates the two different sets of sensory inputs.
source: (2) Similarly, chronic blockade of NMDA receptors during circuit development desegregates the two different sets of sensory inputs, showing that the subcellular targeting of the different afferent inputs to specific regions of a common tectal dendrite requires NMDAR activation (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the MK-801 experiments.

claim: The subcellular targeting of the different afferent inputs to specific regions of a common tectal dendrite requires NMDAR activation.
source: (2) Similarly, chronic blockade of NMDA receptors during circuit development desegregates the two different sets of sensory inputs, showing that the subcellular targeting of the different afferent inputs to specific regions of a common tectal dendrite requires NMDAR activation (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the MK-801 experiments.

claim: Blocking NMDARs after the circuit has formed fails to disrupt the pattern of functional synaptic inputs.
source: (3) Blocking NMDARs after the circuit has formed fails to disrupt the pattern of functional synaptic inputs, indicating a critical period for the sculpting of lamina and the subcellular pattern of targeting of axonal inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding from the late MK-801 experiments.

claim: Monocular enucleation studies in the axolotl showed that eye enucleation during embryonic stages resulted in a portion of the non-visual inputs to shift into the vacant area of the optic tectum.
source: Similar monocular enucleation studies in the axolotl (Harris, 1983) and the rodent (Rhoades, 1980; Rhoades et al., 1981) are consistent with our findings. In both of these studies, eye enucleation during embryonic stages of development resulted in a portion of the non-visual inputs to shift into the vacant area of the optic tectum for the axolotl, and the superior colliculus in the rodent.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Monocular enucleation studies in the rodent showed that eye enucleation during embryonic stages resulted in a portion of the non-visual inputs to shift into the vacant area of the superior colliculus.
source: Similar monocular enucleation studies in the axolotl (Harris, 1983) and the rodent (Rhoades, 1980; Rhoades et al., 1981) are consistent with our findings. In both of these studies, eye enucleation during embryonic stages of development resulted in a portion of the non-visual inputs to shift into the vacant area of the optic tectum for the axolotl, and the superior colliculus in the rodent.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In cats and primates, monocular enucleation leads to the inputs from the remaining eye to grow beyond their normal laminae in the lateral geniculate nucleus.
source: In cats and primates monocular enucleation leads to the inputs from the remaining eye to grow beyond their normal laminae in the lateral geniculate nucleus and take over territory that normally would have been occupied by the enucleated eye (Rakic, 1981; Chalupa and Williams, 1984; Shatz, 1996; Shatz and Sretavan, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The sensory-dependent subcellular targeting of axons to specific regions of a common dendrite is likely not guided by guidance molecules, such as ephrins, alone.
source: The monocular enucleation experiment data also provide evidence that in the tadpole tectum, the sensory-dependent subcellular targeting of axons to specific regions of a common dendrite is likely not guided by guidance molecules, such as ephrins, alone because if it were, then just removing the RGC input would not be expected to desegregate the remaining input.
evidence: This is inferred from the enucleation experimental results.

claim: In the mouse thalamus, cutting the auditory afferent input induced the RGC inputs to shift over to the MGN only in an EphrinA2/A5 double knockout mouse.
source: A rewiring study by Lyckman and colleagues (Lyckman et al., 2001) provides an example of what we may have expected to find if the segregation of sensory inputs in the tadpole optic tectum were regulated by a molecular signal: in the mouse thalamus, RGCs project to the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) and auditory inputs project to the medial geniculate nucleus (MGN). It was found that cutting the auditory afferent input induced the RGC inputs to shift over to the MGN only in an EphrinA2/A5 double knockout mouse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The shift of RGC inputs to MGN was not observed in wild type mice because Ephrin expression between the LGN and MGN inhibits the remaining input from crossing over into vacant territory.
source: The shift was not observed in wild type mice because Ephrin expression between the LGN and MGN inhibits the remaining input from crossing over into vacant territory.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A differential pattern of ephrin expression across the laminar axis of both the Rana pipiens and Xenopus laevis optic tectum has been reported.
source: Nevertheless, the possibility that the absence of the RGC input somehow altered the expression pattern of some putative molecular signal cannot be ruled out, and it is interesting to note that a differential pattern of ephrin expression across the laminar axis of both the Rana pipiens (Scalia and Feldheim, 2005) and Xenopus laevis (Higenell et al., 2012) optic tectum has been reported, although whether this gradient is involved with segregation of the different sensory inputs has not been determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The subcellular segregation of inputs across tectal neuron dendrites could be governed by an NMDAR-dependent correlation-based mechanism similar to the mechanism underlying refinement of the topographic map.
source: The second main finding is that blocking NMDARs with MK-801 during the development of these circuits also disrupts the normal degree of segregation between inputs. These data suggest that the subcellular segregation of inputs across tectal neuron dendrites could be governed by an NMDAR-dependent correlation-based mechanism similar to the mechanism underlying refinement of the topographic map (Cline and Constantine-Paton, 1989; Debski et al., 1990; Dong et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: RGC inputs form a subcellular map across individual tectal neurons such that near-neighbor RGC inputs target to near neighbor region of dendrite.
source: This concept of correlated inputs wiring to common regions of dendrite is supported by the finding that RGC inputs form a subcellular map across individual tectal neurons such that near-neighbor RGC inputs, which would display a high degree of correlated firing, target to near neighbor region of dendrite (Bollmann and Engert, 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The super-correlated pattern of RGC firing created by optic flow across the retina has been shown to enhance refinement.
source: and further the super-correlated pattern of RGC firing created by optic flow across the retina has been shown to enhance refinement (Hiramoto and Cline, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Weak synapses do not support the stabilization of their axon.
source: And because weak synapses do not support the stabilization of its axon (Ruthazer et al., 2006) – the entire HB axon and its synapses would be eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Postsynaptic activation of CaMKII in cultured cortical neurons has been shown to remodel inputs such that the strongest inputs are kept and strengthened while other inputs are completely lost.
source: In addition, this will be an especially interesting experiment given that postsynaptic activation of CaMKII in cultured cortical neurons has been shown to remodel inputs such that the strongest inputs are kept and strengthened while other inputs are completely lost (Pratt et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The guidance and targeting of different sensory inputs is almost certainly achieved by activity-independent molecular cues.
source: Thus, similar to the formation of the topographic map, the guidance and targeting of different sensory inputs is almost certainly achieved by activity-independent molecular cues.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inputs retain their general targeting pattern even with NMDAR blockade.

claim: The normal degree of segregation of inputs at the more local, synaptic level requires NMDAR-dependent activity.
source: But our data also indicate that, similar to the activity-dependent refinement phase of topographic map formation, the normal degree of segregation of inputs at the more local, synaptic level requires NMDAR-dependent activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: The different sensory inputs appear segregated ab initio, from the very beginning.
source: Instead of starting out coarse like the initial topographic map, meaning that the axons are less focused in space such that one postsynaptic neuron receives input from many axons and being sculpted via activity such that any one neuron receives fewer different axonal inputs, the different sensory inputs appear segregated ab initio, from the very beginning (Deeg et al., 2009; Hiramoto and Cline, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Blocking NMDAR activation while the sensory inputs are in the midst of forming synapses with postsynaptic targets causes the inputs to lose their normal degree of segregation.
source: Thus, it is not that the inputs start out overlapping and then become refined by activity, but blocking NMDAR activation while the sensory inputs are in the midst of forming synapses with postsynaptic targets causes the inputs to lose their normal degree of segregation.
evidence: This is a summary of the main experimental finding.

claim: NMDAR-dependent activity prevents the desegregation of inputs.
source: In this context, therefore, NMDAR-dependent activity prevents the desegregation of inputs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: The desegregation of inputs induced by blocking NMDARs is defined by a critical period.
source: Similar to the remodeling of axonal inputs underlying ocular dominance plasticity, the desegregation of inputs induced by blocking NMDARs also appears to be defined by a critical period.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of early versus late NMDAR blockade.

claim: The critical period appears to coincide with when the sensory inputs are forming synaptic connections with postsynaptic tectal neurons.
source: The critical period appears to coincide with when the sensory inputs are forming synaptic connections with postsynaptic tectal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of when early MK-801 exposure has effects.

claim: Late MK-801 exposure could reflect a subpopulation of relatively immature axons that have more recently entered the tectum and are still undergoing NMDAR-dependent correlation-based processes.
source: This increase in overlap in response to late MK801 exposure could reflect a subpopulation of relatively immature axons that have more recently entered the tectum and are still undergoing NMDAR-dependent correlation-based processes.
evidence: This is speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Synapses made by non-visual mechanosensory inputs mature slower and display lower AMPA:NMDA ratios compared to retinotectal synapses.
source: This is consistent with the report that synapses made by non-visual mechanosensory inputs mature slower and display lower AMPA:NMDA ratios compared to retinotectal synapses (Deeg et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In the tadpole optic tectum, inputs are segregated to the distal and proximal regions of a common dendrite.
source: One important aspect of the tadpole optic tectum that sets it apart from most other integration centers is that the tectal neuron dendrites span the entire laminar axis and receive input from both sensory modalities. Thus, in the tadpole optic tectum, inputs are segregated to the distal and proximal regions of a common dendrite, while in zebrafish, and chick, inputs form onto specific cell types (Yamagata and Sanes, 1995; Baier, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the tadpole optic tectum and is supported by citations.

claim: In zebrafish and chick, inputs form onto specific cell types.
source: Thus, in the tadpole optic tectum, inputs are segregated to the distal and proximal regions of a common dendrite, while in zebrafish, and chick, inputs form onto specific cell types (Yamagata and Sanes, 1995; Baier, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the hippocampus, individual pyramidal neurons receive two distinct, spatially segregated sets of afferent input: entorhinal cortical input which innervates the distal region, and local commissural input which is targeted to the more proximal region of the same dendrite.
source: The subcellular type of targeting of inputs that occurs in the tadpole optic tectum also occurs in the hippocampus where individual pyramidal neurons receive two distinct, spatially segregated sets of afferent input: entorhinal cortical input which innervates the distal region, and local commissural input which is targeted to the more proximal region of the same dendrite (Supèr and Soriano, 1994; Supèr et al., 1998; del Río et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Clustered input, as opposed to a disperse pattern, is thought to potentiate spike-timing plasticity processes.
source: Clustered input, as opposed to a disperse pattern, is thought to potentiate spike-timing plasticity processes (Sjostrom et al., 2008) which are expressed in these neurons (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Spike-timing plasticity processes are expressed in tectal neurons.
source: Clustered input, as opposed to a disperse pattern, is thought to potentiate spike-timing plasticity processes (Sjostrom et al., 2008) which are expressed in these neurons (Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Clustering of correlated synaptic input onto a defined region of the dendritic tree could promote cooperation between correlated inputs which may lead to long-lasting changes in synaptic strength.
source: This clustering could promote cooperation between correlated inputs which may lead to long-lasting changes in synaptic strength (Frick et al., 2004) and dendritic excitability (Losonczy et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Clustering of correlated synaptic input onto a defined region of the dendritic tree could promote cooperation between correlated inputs which may lead to changes in dendritic excitability.
source: This clustering could promote cooperation between correlated inputs which may lead to long-lasting changes in synaptic strength (Frick et al., 2004) and dendritic excitability (Losonczy et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.
